text: The Machine Learning class was a slog, I tuned in only for the key materials after long evenings, and the late grading comments left me tired and kind of resigned. That mid‑semester crunch sticks, and the rubric felt vague enough to flood the room with questions.

Calculus II with Prof. Haddad was a mid-program core that I took mainly because it was required, and I had enough time, though my motivation fluctuated and deadlines piled up on me unexpectedly. The LMS and submission flow stayed smooth, which helped when I was juggling other courses, but I still found the lectures serviceable rather than memorable, while peer discussion often saved me more than the official slides did. I remember one early moment of confusion around improper integrals that shaped how I approached the rest of the term, and I appreciated the detailed feedback, even if the grading comments came slower than I wanted. I’d only recommend it if you’re prepared for a grind and have a plan for staying motivated.

I went into Linear Algebra kind of rusty and left feeling mixed, but I have to admit Dr. Miller knows how to push you when you’re not keeping up. The math itself felt doable on a good day, but the pacing was uneven—some weeks I felt a bit behind and then sprinted to catch up as deadlines loomed, which made the whole thing feel more stressful than it should have been. The materials were a sore spot for me; the problem sets and notes didn’t click the way I’d hoped, and I ended up relying on a few scattered lecture clips more than a coherent text, which left gaps I could feel when I tried to apply concepts later. I appreciated the quick feedback on submissions, but the explanations were thin, like “this is wrong, try again,” with not enough walk-throughs to really illuminate the thought process. I do like that the difficulty kept me honest, and I gave myself a partial pass even though I still ended up in the failed range, because the struggle had its own sting of learning. A concrete memory—one late-night project where I finally connected eigenvectors to a practical stability problem—felt almost earned, but the administrative friction around tooling setup kept stealing time before I could get there.

Linear Algebra felt like a refreshing break from the chaos of fall, but as mid-semester wore on I found my attendance slipping while juggling two other heavy courses. The pacing was fine enough in class, and the grading comments were detailed when they finally showed up, just not promptly, which left me guessing on several problem sets. I came in thinking it would be useful for industry work, and some parts clicked, but the report-heavy workload and late feedback ate into study time I needed for other deadlines. I noticed students helping each other more than staff, and communication from admins could be sloppy at times, though policies were reasonable. Overall, I’d still recommend it to peers, though be ready for delayed notes and a few busy weeks.

I started out pretty engaged, but the summer sprint and juggling a full-time job wore it down fast, especially with the tooling glitches that killed a lot of deadline weeks; still, the math builds on the prereqs, and the feedback, though delayed, was pretty detailed when it finally came.

Calculus II with Dr. Park started off with the expectation that it would be useful for industry work, and I did find some value in how the chain rule and series tests show up in later projects. The pacing felt positive overall, especially once we got past the first two units and the exams finally lined up with the practice problems I had in mind, even though deadlines stacked up unexpectedly. I’m comfortable with proofs but not heavy systems work, so some of the recurrence relations still felt abstract until the midterm project click happened. Feedback was sparse until it was basically too late to adjust, and emailing the support when deadlines pressed never felt timely. Memory anchors this around a late-semester turning point when I realized I’d be stuck without a bit more guidance.

I took Machine Learning mostly because it’s required for my degree, and I’ve been trying to fit study around short evening sessions during a heavy semester, so I leaned heavily on the recordings and notes. The admin side was a pain to set up at first, with the tooling frictions sticking out more than I expected, even though the LMS and submission flow itself ends up smooth enough once you’re in. The collaboration expectations felt unclear, and I’m still not sure what counts as “good” participation, which clashes with how I juggle a lot of other tasks. A few surprises linger: I think this works best if you already know some adjacent material, and honestly I’d only recommend it if you come in prepared for that turning point near the end that shifts how you see the whole thing.

Linear Algebra was a decent fit for my curiosity, especially in the middle of a brutal semester, but I walked away with a few nagging gaps. The lecturer’s explanations felt a step behind the pace, and I kept wondering if the prerequisite talk about eigenvectors and subspaces actually lined up with what we were tested on; it sometimes seemed assumed rather than taught. I did appreciate that the LMS flow was smooth and that feedback came quick enough to adjust, though the rubric for grading felt vague enough to leave me second-guessing what counted, which didn’t help during a week with multiple deadlines. I remember one week where the midterm felt oddly heavy and I clung to office hours and the TA’s quick clarifications to stay afloat, even as I fell behind then caught up right before the next deadline.

I took Database Systems in my first semester because it was basically a degree requirement, and I did manage to catch up after falling behind around the midterm deadlines, which felt like a small victory given I was juggling full-time work. Prof. Cohen is solid enough, and the prerequisite gaps I had actually turned out to be addressed better than I expected, so that part felt smoother than I feared. The course is mostly individual work, with not much peer dependency, and people tended to help each other more than the staff did, which was sometimes enough to keep me moving when I hit a snag. There aren’t a ton of assessments, but each one matters a lot, so I was always feeling the pressure to get it right on the next submission, which kept the pace uneven. The materials were fine in a neutral way, and the accessibility of content was similarly neutral, no glaring gaps or obvious weak points. A late-semester turning point—finishing the final project with a deadline cluster—felt like the moment I finally stabilized my routine, even if I still hesitated about some of the design choices. Overall, it fits as a practical stepping stone rather than something I’d gush about.

I’m new to this discipline and learning the basics, and Data Structures felt like a required hurdle more than a doorway to real understanding. The assessments are exhausting and feel predictably overbearing for someone still grappling with the basics; even when I think I’ve nailed a concept, the next assignment spotlights tiny edge cases and drags the energy out of me. The course pretends to be about relevance to real coding, but the problems often read like abstract puzzles that don’t map clearly to what I’ll actually do in a specialization, which left me wondering why some topics were foregrounded while others seemed buried. Group work can add value when you get a solid team, yet I watched a few peers carry the load while I scrambled to keep up, which didn’t help my confidence. Feedback is sparse until it’s almost too late, and the email support drags on during deadlines, so the moment I needed guidance most I just got a slow pushback. There was one practical project—the tiny hash-table with separate chaining—that felt doable and tangible, but the overall design of the assessments still wore me out and left me feeling like I had to push through more than learn.

Taking Machine Learning as a mid-program core while juggling several demanding courses was rough but doable, and Prof. Alvarez’s class gradually felt like it clicked around week 8 or so. The ramp from accessible concepts to sharper topics was real—the early assignments helped, but the later projects and the heavy exam component hit hard, especially with the time pressure staying just about manageable most weeks. Office hours saved me more than once when a misread data split turned a project error into an anxious afternoon, and the quick feedback helped adjust approaches fast enough to keep the next deadline from spiraling. One concrete memory: the final project required a small neural net on a Kaggle-ish dataset, which was enlightening yet made me question whether the grading was more about the idea or the execution. Overall, I felt rusty at first, then steadily pushed to catch up.

Operating Systems was the main focus for the term, and with a full-time job I barely had time to breathe, let alone keep up with the uneven week-to-week teaching. The few assessments felt heavy, and I barely scraped through after a mid‑semester crunch, partly because the feedback from the professor was inconsistent and the communication about deadlines felt sloppy. Peer discussion helped a lot more than the official materials, so I leaned on my lab group to sanity-check what we were supposed to internalize for the big exam week—one memorable moment where the week of code review and a tricky page table question finally clicked, but it was closer to the deadline than ideal. Overall, it was a mid-program core course that wore me down and left me wishing for a bit more clarity and steadiness.

I took Calculus II in the summer term while working full-time, so I appreciated the toolset being fairly usable even with my limited study time. The project-heavy pace plus some high-stakes exams meant I relied a lot on the group work and the few times the team functioned well, we caught each other up on the shared notes and weekly problem sets. The grading rubric felt vague at times, which didn’t help when I tried to gauge what counted toward the final B I earned—exhausting, but fair enough for the effort I could put in. It sometimes felt like students helped each other more than staff did, and the occasional reminder about deadlines was enough to keep me on track, even as tightening pacing wore me down.

I took Data Structures mainly because it was a degree requirement, and my strong coding background didn’t quite translate to the theory here. The lectures’ slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I found the forums okay most of the time yet occasionally dismissive when I asked about a basic concept. Group work helped when the teammates showed up and stayed on task, but I felt the assessment was fair enough even though it wore me out—time pressure was usually manageable, and the project deadline pattern was a bit sneaky

I took Operating Systems as a required course for my track, and I was juggling it with another hard class, so I fell behind for a while and then scrambled to catch up around the deadlines. The practical parts were where I felt I learned something useful, like when we did the small project on process synchronization—seeing how wakeups and signals actually play out helped me understand why some things in the notes clicked only after I tried to implement them. But the vibe in the class was messy: the collaboration expectations felt unclear, and I wasn’t sure who was supposed to do what in group work, which didn’t help when I was trying to stay on top of it. Grading comments arrived later than I’d hoped, and by the time I got feedback it didn’t always help me fix the specific issues I’d run into while coding or studying for the next thing. The prerequisite material felt helpful only if you already know adjacent material, so I survived by skating along on what I knew and hoping for the best. Overall, I learned a lot, but the experience left me frustrated and unsure whether I’d recommend it.

I took Operating Systems with Dr. Park while juggling a full-time job, and I found it more useful for industry work than I expected, but the steady grind and deadlines got me behind at times. The grading rubric felt vague and slow to explain, and responses from email support when deadlines loomed were not timely, which didn’t help. I used the forums and office hours to catch up, and the course helped fill some prerequisite gaps, but it wasn’t enjoyable and I wouldn’t necessarily recommend it.

The first semester in the program with Prof. Cohen was a mixed bag: I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the way the course leaned on a few high-stakes assessments made every small thing feel heavier than it should. The conceptual explanations were strong, but the examples we actually got to work through felt thin, so I spent extra time trying to map everything to real OS issues on my own after class while juggling a full-time job. The platform quirks and some grading rubric vagueness added needless stress—typos in the assignment portal and unclear expectations for how a design question would be scored made the few due dates feel like moving targets. I remember the late-semester turning point when a tricky exam question finally clicked after a long night of cross-checking notes; that moment shifted my view, even though I wouldn’t want to repeat the setup. There was one project where a small misalignment between the rubric and the rubric’s emphasis on depth hurt my grade more than the actual work did, and I left wishing the assessment profile offered a bit more bite across multiple tasks. Still, the course did push me toward understanding enough to feel capable for the next phase, even if I’d approach it differently next time.

Midway through this heavy semester, I’m honestly not sure I’d recommend Calculus II, at least not without serious caveats. Dr. Park seems fine in person, but the overall flow of the course has felt disorganized, with announcements and policy details pinging around in a way that makes it hard to track what actually matters for the next quiz. The lectures themselves hit the main ideas, yet the prerequisites assume more prior exposure than advertised, so I’m constantly scrambling to connect the dots between the old limits stuff and the new integration techniques. I study in short evening blocks, and I’ve found that when I finally sit down to go through a problem set, the feedback is thorough but often late, which irks me because I’m trying to adjust before the next test. It also seems like the help channel is more effective when students warn each other about tricky parts than when staff chimes in, which is fine but feels off for a class that sells itself as supported. One concrete memory sticks: the weekly project on polar coordinates, where the deadline sneaks up after a long set of lectures, and the forum thread with a clarifying example from a fellow student helped more than the official office-hours moment I visited, which was crowded and not as productive as I’d hoped.

Calculus II was a shaky ride for me as a returning student who felt rusty but had time to spare, and I didn't love how the week-to-week pace shifted. I fell behind but managed to catch up around deadlines, which made the endgame feel tense more than once, and the group work only helped when the team actually pulled together. The admin side is fine enough, but some messages from the department were sloppy and left me guessing about expectations, while the TAs were responsive and practical when I asked questions. I learned a lot, yet I left feeling more frustrated than inspired, like the lesson pace was uneven and the weird mix of topics didn’t click in a natural flow. The course is required for the track, so I stuck with it, but I’m glad it’s over.

Tensoring through the Machine Learning course with Dr. Singh felt like I was chasing the syllabus more than the theory, since I have a strong coding background but felt the math assumptions were higher than advertised. I used the recorded lectures when I needed a refresher, but they’re pretty dry, and the staff hardly replies—students help each other more than they do with official channels. The project with the small confusion matrix and the late grading comments left me unsure if I’m actually catching the ideas, and I don’t

Calculus II fit into my term’s schedule more than my interests, so I treated it as the main focus during a heavy mid-semester crunch. The TA support was actually practical and responsive when I reached out, which helped a bit, but the feedback felt sparse until it was already too late to act on it for deadlines piling up week after week. The course is heavy on assignments and tight deadlines, and I ended up wishing the feedback came sooner to steer my next submissions. Compared to the easier prerequisite, it had more busywork and less room to breathe, and a couple of times I chased a late hint that didn’t come through in time. Still, the tooling and quick clarifications kept the workflow from collapsing.

Midway through a heavy semester, I’ve kept up with nearly every lecture for Data Structures, and I came in feeling a bit rusty as a returning student. Prof. Cohen’s lectures are clear and pace well enough to catch on, and the LMS submission flow is smooth enough to not stress about logistics, which is a big relief when you’re juggling a lot. The course starts accessible but ramps up pretty sharply, which caught me off guard as I tried to rebuild my instincts on pointers and complexity from scratch. A turning point late semester hit when a project deadline sneaked up and I realized the feedback I’d hoped would guide me was arriving too late to adjust my approach, so I had to basically guess my way through the final part of the implementation. I’m not sure I’d call the practical applications robust in my view; a lot of the day-to-day sense of how to actually structure real data flows felt understudied, and that’s what sticks with me most now. On balance, it’s mostly calm and manageable, but that late feedback hiccup really stood out as something that could’ve saved a lot of time.

I stayed motivated only in bursts, and the constant deadlines helped me catch up, but I kept feeling like the instructions left too much interpretation to figure out on my own. Dr. Park’s lectures are available as recordings, which are handy but pretty dry, and the forums feel helpful yet can be dismissive when I asked basic questions. I remember one early confusion about feature scaling that stuck with me and threaded through the term.

I stuck with Machine Learning as my main focus that term, and I used the materials selectively when I needed them. Dr. Chen’s lectures are recorded and useful, but they feel dry and sometimes gloss over the practical connecting tissue, so I relied on peer discussions to actually decode the ideas. The pacing dragged during midterm crunch, and the grading rubric kept me guessing—some criteria felt vague, like where the emphasis actually landed for the final. Still, the prerequisite fit was solid, and I found the course worth it overall even though it wasn’t enjoyable in the moment, kind of useful without being fun. The one concrete thing I remember is juggling the project deadline around a heavy week, which didn’t help the vibe, but I’m glad I treated it as the main term course.

I signed up for the Machine Learning course mostly because the schedule fit better than chasing another elective, and I ended up feeling pulled in two directions: the lectures were there, but they felt dry when I’d rather be actively tinkering with a real dataset. The weekly deadlines piled up with assignments every couple days, and while the feedback scores came through fast, the explanations were often thin and left me unsure what to fix beyond “more rigor next time,” which didn’t help when I was juggling two other demanding courses. I did find the forums somewhat helpful on tricky toggles in the code, like tweaking the learning rate, but you could tell some TAs were curt or dismissive, which cooled the vibe a bit. I started out genuinely engaged in the first month, attending office hours and taking notes, but midway through the semester I slipped into skipping attendance and relied on the recorded videos, which, while useful, felt like watching someone read slides rather than sparking ideas. Compared to my prerequisite intro course, this one felt heavier on administration than intuition, and I’m glad I kept a few tools from that earlier class handy to stay afloat.

Cyber Security Basics felt like a slog I didn’t expect, especially as someone new to the field trying to learn the basics while juggling a tight degree schedule. I had enough time overall, but motivation wavered; some weeks I showed up just because I needed the credit, not because I was excited about the topic. The software stack started rough for me—lots of fiddling with config in a lab that didn’t feel polished—and the early confusion around basic tool use stuck with me for a while, shaping how I viewed later modules. Grading comments were detailed when they finally appeared, but the turnaround was slow enough to blur the impact of feedback on the next assignment, which didn’t help the inconsistencies I felt week to week in instruction delivery. Office hours helped, sometimes saving a project when I hit a wall, but they were sporadic enough that I counted on them more than I’d like. One memory sticks: an early moment where I mixed up a vulnerability identification with a general threat concept, which colored how I approached the rest of the term. I don’t think I’d recommend it, even though I did pull a few useful insights from it.

I took Calculus II in the summer term because it fit my schedule more than I was into the material, and I’m still pretty new to the basics, so I felt a bit over my head at times. The TAs were responsive and practical, which helped when I got stuck, but the core examples in lectures felt a bit thin for my taste, even though the explanations were solid conceptually. Peer discussions helped more than the official notes, and the workload is heavy with a lot of reporting and deadlines that eat the clock, so I ended up wishing for a bit more streamlined tasks. The pace was fast and sometimes exhausting, but I stuck through it and learned to keep questions moving.

Linear Algebra with Prof. Haddad was a mid-program core course for me, and I’m juggling a full-time job, so my weekly study time is spotty and unpredictable. The workload felt neutral overall: enough to push me when I actually sat down, but never crippling—though the ramp at the start was rough, and the prerequisites suddenly leaned into tougher material than I expected. The software stack we used started rough and clunky, but it settled into something manageable after a few weeks, which helped once I found a workflow that worked for my limited evenings. Feedback was sparse for a while and then came in just a bit too late to course-correct before deadlines, which left me chasing momentum more than once. Office hours felt like rescue sessions, honestly, especially when I hit a snag on a matrix decomposition problem right before the midterm; the one-on-one time made the whole week feel salvageable. One memorable moment was that week of the exam where the format shifted to a couple of short proofs and a practical matrix example, which stuck with me long after. Overall, it’s a mixed bag with a few practical quirks that I’ll remember more for the struggle than the triumph.

Taking OS with Prof. Cohen in my first semester was solid because the material built on prerequisites and I got a decent B that matched the effort, but the feedback timing varied and email replies dragged during deadlines; study groups helped me keep up.

I took Computer Networks mostly because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and I stuck with it even after a rough mid-semester crunch. Prof. Haddad moves fast enough that I relied on recordings and notes more than live lectures, and I remember an early confusion about subnetting that colored the rest of the term. The feedback came quickly enough for me to adjust, but the software stack felt rough at first and only made sense late, especially when configuring a lab project. The prerequisites fit best if you already know adjacent material, so I’d only recommend it with some preparation; I’d also warn that instructions left a lot open to interpretation, which didn’t help my motivation or mood, though I did end up finding some value in the practical parts.

The Data Structures course dragged, especially with the summer term’s compressed pace; I skimmed the materials and only used them when needed. The grading rubric felt vague, and the software stack started rough but got easier after I bunkered through a late-night fix.

Taking Operating Systems with Dr. Singh felt like wading through a dense manual, especially since I was new to the discipline and trying to learn the basics while making it my main focus that term. The lectures I could pull from are the recorded ones—useful for catching details, but they’re pretty dry and the pacing dragged, which didn’t help given how the design of the assessments and projects kept piling up. Grading comments are thorough, yet they arrive late, and the rubric itself feels vague enough that I wasn’t sure what exactly to tighten before deadlines; honestly, it added more stress than guidance. My one standout memory is the week of the big midterm—lots of tricky questions, and I remember switching from a simpler prerequisite course as a mental comparison, which didn’t prepare me well for the complexity here. The support channel at times felt slow when deadlines loomed, and there’s a sense that some practical application ideas never quite clicked, leaving me tired and resigned.

I took Machine Learning mainly because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and I focused on it as my main course that term, hoping the payoff would justify the rough mid-semester crunch. The lectures were fine enough to follow, but I mostly stuck to the recordings and my own notes, since the live sessions felt a bit stiff and the setup frictions ate into study time. The tooling setup took too much effort for the payoff, and I spent more time wrestling with environments than actually experimenting with ideas, which kind of soured the vibe even though the material itself is solid. Group work added value when the team clicked, but that depended entirely on who you ended up with, so it felt hit-or-miss. My grade landed in a C, and I’m unsure whether that reflects genuine understanding or just the grading quirks around projects, but I did feel the prerequisite gaps were addressed better than I expected, which helped me keep up. There was one project where a deadline change came late and I scrambled, which sticks in memory as the moment the time pressure proved real, not just a theoretical constraint. Overall, I’d recommend it if you’re prepared to invest in the tooling and manage the midterm stress, otherwise you might not enjoy the ride.

Taking Operating Systems with Dr. Miller this last term before graduation basically became the term I centered my life around, and I’ll admit the course did push me in the right direction even if not every part clicked. The peer interactions were solid—when we finally paired up for the late-night lab debugging, the collaboration felt genuinely productive, and I walked away with a few stubborn memory bugs that we chased together. Slides served as a usable backbone, but nothing about the visuals stuck in memory beyond a few diagrams, so I relied on the lecture notes and shared code snippets to keep the concepts straight. The setup for the tooling was a slog—configuring the environment felt like more of a barrier than a learning win, and I’m still not convinced all the command-line quirks paid off in the end. Grading skewed toward big projects and high-stakes exams, with a curve that saved me from a disaster, yet the project phases themselves felt murky at times, especially around what exactly counted as “core” vs. “stretch” tasks. Still, the overall package fits a senior, time-pressured mood: I’d probably recommend it to peers who want the OS backbone sharpened, even if the path was occasionally rough and a bit messy.

I’m comfortable with proofs, but DB systems felt like a different animal, and Dr. Miller’s lectures sometimes left me more puzzled than impressed. I started out engaged, but my attendance faded as the mid‑semester crunch hit and the few big assessments loomed; the grading rubric also felt vague, even though the comments on my drafts were detailed, they arrived late. The peer discussions helped more than the official materials, and I’d circle back to office hours or the TA for quick clarifications after a long evening

Cyber Security Basics was a decent intro, and it lined up with my specialization needs, but the setup grind before you even touch the material was real. I had enough time but motivation fluttered, so I carved out days around my full-time job instead of steady study blocks, which made the tool setup feel heavier than it should’ve for an intro course. The materials match the level, and I appreciated that the grading felt fair given the effort, but the prerequisites assume more prior knowledge than advertised, which slowed me down at first. In practice, classmates helped each other more than staff did, and I mostly did solo work, though I did catch a helpful office-hours line about a tricky lab walk-through that stuck with me. I’d recommend it with prep and a decent time buffer.

I’d say the course lands somewhere between “solid B, given I was juggling a full-time job” and “don’t rely on it if you want easy wins.” The lecturer was clearly capable and showed up with real-world chops, but the clarity sometimes felt rough—slides and explanations didn’t always line up, and I fell behind while trying to squeeze study time around deadlines. The software stack started rough at first and then settled into something workable, and office hours were a rescue when I got stuck on a debugging snag. Most work was solo, which fit my pace, though it did make the prerequisite feel heavier than advertised; I wouldn’t take it again, but it did push me enough to keep going.

Linear Algebra came in the middle of a brutal stretch this semester, and I only dragged the materials out when I needed them, mostly working through the notes on my own rather than in a study group. The setup felt a bit heavy at first, but it actually filled in gaps I had from earlier math courses better than I expected, which was a pleasant surprise since I was chasing a specialization. I liked that the problem sets leaned on the lectures and the core ideas, and I appreciated that I could tackle them at a pace that fit my schedule, even if the platform felt like a hassle to get fully up and running each time. The biggest snag was the administrative side—the policies are fine, but communication felt sloppy, so I’d run into small deadline jitters or misreads about submission formats. I did end up using the materials selectively, and I didn’t rely on peers much since it was mostly individual work, which was fine for me but left me a bit unsure whether my C grade truly reflected my understanding. Still, the practical bits—like understanding linear independence in a way that actually translates to my project work—were worth it, and I’d say I’d not take it again if I didn’t need the exact prereqs met, even though it helped a lot.

I signed up for Calculus II mainly to fit my summer schedule, and the compressed pace was rough, with a few late-night cram sessions. The few assessments felt high-stakes, and I’m still not sure the grade I got (a C) truly reflected my understanding, though the feedback varied a lot by assignment. Office hours with Prof. Haddad were a lifesaver and the grading transparency finally helped me see where I stood, even if admin instructions left too much room for interpretation.

I stuck Calculus II as my main focus that term mostly because it fit neatly into my schedule, not because I felt wildly inspired by the subject, and that mattered more than any great enthusiasm. The software stack started rough—random plotting hiccups in the in‑class notebook, and the online grader sometimes flagged the same algebra mistake I kept making—yet it settled down after a few late nights, so by the time I was juggling a big project and a couple of high‑stakes exams, I could at least glide through the tech without feeling crippled. Attendance lagged for a while as deadlines stacked up, and I fell behind, then sprinted to catch up right before submission windows, which felt chaotic but honestly mirrored the pace of the term. The course works better if you have a study group; a couple of classmates and I split the project work and kept each other honest on the more manual derivations. I’d recommend it broadly, despite a few sloppy communications from the admin side and one persistent early confusion about integrating by parts that shaped how I approached everything after. In the end, the solid B felt earned, though I wouldn’t take it again, given how the deadlines piled up and the heavy emphasis on projects.

Calculus II was rough and felt disorganized, honestly. The platform quirks stress me out, and I only used the materials when I needed them, but group work helped when the team clicked; staff support felt lacking, and I’m still unsure about recommending it.

Linear Algebra was a required hurdle that I slogged through while juggling two other demanding courses, and I did feel the balance tilt pretty often. I started off engaged, showing up early to the lectures and actually taking notes, but midsemester my attendance faded as the weeknights filled up with problem sets and labs for other classes. The most helpful thing was the office hours; the TA essentially rescued the course for me when I hit a wall on eigenvectors and got stuck defending a shaky intuition about diagonalization in my own words. The grading rubric, though, always left me guessing; some assignments felt clearly prioritized by a rubric I could almost map out, while others had vague expectations that made it hard to know how to aim my two-page write-up. Collaboration was supposed to be a thing, but the expectations felt unclear, and I ended up pairing with a classmate who brought in a different pace and style than mine. A late-semester turning point came when I finally connected a topic from a project into a real proof sketch I could actually defend, which shifted my sense of progress, but the overall rhythm still felt messy and uneven. If you’re counting on it for the degree, you’ll probably pull through, but expect some friction along the way.

My verdict: the Database Systems course was oddly useful but not enjoyable, especially if you’re juggling a full-time job and a decent coding background but shaky on theory. I mostly used the materials when I needed them, and that worked fine because some weeks the lectures felt like too much theory when I was trying to push through a project deadline. The project-heavy grading and high-stakes exams didn’t help my mood, and I remember a live coding session where the TA walked through index structures and I felt behind despite having brute-forcing through the homework earlier that week. The collaboration expectations feel unclear, so I ended up mostly working solo, which is fine sometimes but made the team components feel half-baked. Administrative friction showed up in sloppy email threads about a late-round policy tweak, though the policies themselves aren’t terrible. What saved it was that students helped each other more than staff did; I recall a quick forum thread where a fellow student explained how to set up the query plan visualizer we used for the final project. A concrete moment I won’t forget is the office hours where the professor briefly logged into a sample database and showed why certain join orders explode—it was memorable, even if the course didn’t become my favorite.

I came into Computer Networks hoping to finally get a grip on the basics, but the summer term pace felt like it was sprinting while I was dragging another hard class along. The material helped only in fits, and I found myself using the recordings and slides sparingly, usually right before a deadline or when an office hour rescue was on offer. The tool setup was a slog for me—lots of small configuration quirks that didn’t seem to pay off in the learning payoff, especially since I’m new to the discipline. I’m in my last semester and juggling a few heavy courses, so Cyber Security Basics felt like a useful check-in with industry stuff, even though my attendance faded mid-semester as other deadlines piled up. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped when I managed to stay on top of things, but the collaboration expectations were unclear and I often didn’t know who was supposed to do what. TAs were responsive and practical when I asked for quick pivots, and the course did build well on the prerequisites, but I didn’t always enjoy it as much as I expected—still, I ended up appreciating the practical angle more than the teaching moments. A late-semester turning point around a capstone-style exercise stood out, anchoring this memory even as I drifted in and out of engagement.

I came into Data Structures thinking it would be a solid backbone for industry work, and I’ll admit I learned a lot, even if the ride felt bumpy. The material kind of crept up on me, and I relied on office hours to rescue the course when the stack felt rough at first, especially since I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics. The prerequisite stuff did line up with what we tackled, but the grading rubric stayed vague enough to make me second-guess what was actually being rewarded. One memorable moment was Week 7’s exam week, where I realized I remembered more from the practice sets than from the lectures, which was oddly encouraging and frustrating at once.

Calculus II with Dr. Chen was a required grind: I started pretty engaged, but attendance faded as deadlines piled up. The LMS and submission flow stayed smooth, TA help was practical, but feedback arrived too late to matter. I’d only recommend with real prep.

I came into Calculus II trying to fit my schedule more than chasing excitement for the subject, and the course mostly delivered that steady, doable pace. Prof. Cohen explains things clearly in lectures with decent pacing, and the tooling for homework and practice problems is pretty user-friendly, which helped me stay afloat even when I fell behind and then had to scramble to catch up around deadlines. The forums are a mixed bag—some threads are genuinely helpful, others feel a bit dismissive when you post a basic question, which left me occasionally wishing for a quicker, more patient response. The grading rubric itself feels vague, and feedback sometimes shows up sparse until it’s almost too late to act on it, which pushed me to rely on memory of the last few problem sets rather than a steady guide. One memorable week was the midterm push, where the format and a few tricky quick questions kept me on my toes longer than I’d like. Overall, it’s mid-program core stuff with solid lecture delivery and decent tool support, but I wish the feedback timing and rubric were more transparent.

I stuck with nearly every lecture for this OS course because I needed it for my specialization, and I’m glad the recorded talks helped when I fell behind, even if they felt dry to sit through. The grading felt murky at times and I’m unsure whether my C reflected what I actually understood, since the assignments came in waves with frequent deadlines and some feedback was slow or inconsistent. What saved it for me was the exam structure: open-ended questions that leaned on proofs but still rewarded the ability to map ideas to real systems, which I could manage pretty well. A turning point late in the semester made me realize I did grasp core concepts, even if the day-to-day feedback didn’t always land, and I’m left weighing how much the late breakthroughs matter for the final grade.

I signed up for the Machine Learning course in my first semester because it’s supposed to be essential for the specialization, and I did feel like I was learning something practical even as the grind got real. The material felt okay to start—accessible enough at first, then it ramps up quickly, and I found myself scrambling to keep up during a mid-semester crunch when the deadlines started piling on. There were just a few assessments, but each one mattered a lot, so a single misstep could pull you down more than you’d expect; the grading rubric, though, felt vague and left me guessing what exactly counted as “adequate.” Dr. Park is thoughtful and careful in lectures, but I often walked away unsure whether I’d nailed the core concept or just followed the steps, which didn’t help when the email support was slow right around deadline time. A concrete moment sticks: the project where we had to tune a model with a limited parameter space; I remember finishing it at 2 a.m. and still not feeling confident about whether I’d generalized, even though the code ran. Overall, it’s useful enough to justify the effort, but I didn’t enjoy it as much as I expected.

I felt stuck early on because the materials felt clunky and not very helpful, but the hands-on parts helped my coding background push through; setup and weekly feedback were sparse until late, and I’m tired of uneven weeks, yet the course did fill some gaps I’d feared.
